timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Well, it has been called an epidemic. Diabetes impacts 9 million Canadians at that number is expected to grow.
Many diabetics lose sensation in their feet, making them vulnerable to potentially fatal infections.
It's a serious problem, but a calorie doctor may have found a way to bring those old feelings back.
Bruce Howell first learned he had diabetes 10 years ago, soon after he began noticing problems with his feet.
Just my feet were very, very sensitive and like a tingling sensation.
And then when I went to the diabetes clinic and some of the education that they provide, that's what made me aware of how diabetes does affect your feet.
Over time, high blood sugar can damage nerves and the hands and feet without sensation.
An injury can go unnoticed until it's too late.
These patients end up developing complications such as ulcers.
Those ulcers can become infected, some of those require amputation and some patients actually die from the complications.
Right now patients are told to check for injuries daily, but that's often not enough to avoid infections.
This insole, however, could help.
We're developing an insole and it's a pressure sensing insole for diabetics with peripheral neuropathy.
And when it does is it restores sensation in the feet for people who can't actually feel their feet.
With nerves damaged in the feet, information about pressure and vibrations collected by sensors and delivered to a receiver placed on the patient's back.
Over time, those patients are actually able to rewire their brain to interpret what they're feeling on their back as what they would normally feel on their feet.
Small sensations that could prevent serious injury, the product is still a development, but is scheduled to enter the market by the end of this year.
Bruce is looking forward to it.
Happy for anything that can keep his health in step.
Heather, your ex-global news.
The device is also connected to a watch that can alert the diabetic to any potential problem.

youtube_description: Heather Yourex, Global TV Calgary Heath Reporter, recently visited the Orpyx Medical Technologies Inc. head office to interview Founder & CEO, Dr. Breanne Everett. Dr. Everett explained how she hopes that their technology will dramatically reduce the number of foot complications associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. After 40, at least 30% of diabetics will have lost sensation in their feet. Orpyx' devices, the SurroSense Rx and the SurroGait Rx, will serve as an early detection system to the patient, alerting them of any dangerous pressure areas or damage so they can immediately modify their behaviour and thus, prevent dreaded complications before they occur. For more information, please visit www.orpyx.com.
